title: TTI vs Chervon: Milwaukee and RYOBI against EGO, FLEX and SKIL
seoTitle: TTI vs Chervon: Brands, Results and the Galli Move Compared
dek: Two Hong Kong-listed cordless groups, one former CEO. How Techtronic Industries and Chervon compare on size, brands, retail channels and results, and what Joe Galli's move to Chervon changes.
description: WCB's running comparison of Techtronic Industries (TTI) and Chervon: Milwaukee, RYOBI and Hoover against EGO, FLEX and SKIL, with 2025 and first-half 2026 results, retail channels, ownership and the September 2026 appointment of former TTI chief Joseph Galli as Chervon CEO.

coverCredit.text: Card: World Clean Biz, using the TTI and Chervon company logos

status.label: Galli's first months at Chervon
status.text: Joseph Galli, TTI's chief executive from 2008 to 2024, has run Chervon since 10 September 2026 and has already hired several former TTI and Milwaukee managers. Both are expected to report full-year 2026 results in March 2027.

summary: TTI and Chervon are both Hong Kong-listed groups built on cordless battery platforms, both manufacture in their own factories in Asia, and North America is the largest market for both. The difference is scale. TTI reported USD 8.29 billion of revenue in the first half of 2026; Chervon reported USD 1.03 billion, about one eighth as much.

Their brands meet head to head. Milwaukee competes with FLEX for professional tradespeople, and RYOBI competes with EGO and SKIL for homeowners, especially in battery outdoor equipment. TTI also owns a floorcare business, Hoover in North America, Vax, Oreck and Dirt Devil, which Chervon has no equivalent of. In US home centres the two lean on different retailers: RYOBI's main US retailer is The Home Depot, while Lowe's helped launch EGO, FLEX and SKIL as nationwide home-centre exclusives in 2021.

2026 has narrowed the story more than the numbers. Chervon returned to growth in the first half, with revenue up 12.8% and gross margin up six points to 39.3%, while TTI grew 5.9% with Milwaukee up 10.5% in local currencies. Then in September Chervon's founder Pan Longquan handed the CEO job to Joseph Galli, the man who led TTI for sixteen years. Whether his playbook from Milwaukee can be repeated at FLEX is the question this file follows.

questions.q: Which is bigger, TTI or Chervon?
questions.a: TTI, by a wide margin. TTI reported 2025 revenue of USD 15.26 billion against Chervon's USD 1.63 billion, and USD 8.29 billion against USD 1.03 billion in the first half of 2026. Chervon grew faster in that half, 12.8% against 5.9%, but from a 2025 base that had fallen 8.2%.

questions.q: Which brands compete with each other?
questions.a: Milwaukee and FLEX both target professional tradespeople. RYOBI competes with EGO in battery outdoor equipment and with SKIL in home power tools. TTI's floorcare brands, Hoover in North America, Vax, Oreck and Dirt Devil, have no counterpart among Chervon's own brands.

questions.q: Why does Joseph Galli's move matter?
questions.a: Galli ran TTI from 2008 to 2024, the years in which Milwaukee became one of the leading professional tool brands. Since becoming Chervon's CEO on 10 September 2026 he has hired managers from TTI and Milwaukee and put a former Milwaukee product manager in charge of FLEX professional product development, which points to FLEX as Chervon's main bet against Milwaukee.

Both are listed in Hong Kong. TTI describes the Pudwill family as its largest shareholder; executive chairman Horst Pudwill reported interests of about 21.86% at the end of 2025. Chervon's founder Pan Longquan held 50.92% of voting shares in March 2026 and remains chairman.

Both groups make most products in their own Asian factories. TTI reports manufacturing in China and Vietnam as well as Mexico and the United States; Chervon reports major production in Nanjing, China, and in Vietnam, and FLEX keeps operations in Germany. The factory for a specific model still has to be read from its label.
